frameworks.name: Eight Business Analysis Equations
frameworks.definition: A seven-plus-one framework of arithmetic ratios (LTGP:CAC, gross margin, CAC, ROIC, payback period, sales velocity x LTGP, sales velocity / churn, TAM x LTGP / risk) that together determine a business's current health, scalability ceiling, and opportunity size.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that lifetime gross profit to customer acquisition cost (LTGP:CAC) is the fundamental economic unit of any business: all profit generated by the business flows from this single ratio, making it the first and most important metric to establish before evaluating any other business variable.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: All profit in a business comes from the spread between what it costs to acquire a customer and what that customer generates in gross profit over their lifetime; every other metric is downstream of this ratio.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi specifies that a minimum LTGP:CAC ratio of 3:1 is required to have enough margin to scale a business; ratios below 3:1 indicate the business is too constrained to grow, while a ratio of 5:1 or higher is strong and can offset weakness in other metrics.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi

anchors.value: too constrained to scale — reject the business
strong — can forgive other weak metrics

bounded_by: Does not distinguish between passive and active-operator investments; context is businesses where the analyst is actively involved

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that using lifetime revenue (LTV) instead of lifetime gross profit (LTGP) to evaluate customer acquisition economics is a critical mistake for businesses with non-software cost structures, because gross margins below ~100% mean that revenue overstates the actual spread available to fund growth.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.speaker_term: lifetime value vs lifetime gross profit
conditions: Businesses with physical products, labor, inventory, or manufacturing costs — i.e., gross margins below ~100%
Software and SaaS businesses are the exception where LTV and LTGP effectively converge
claims.mechanism: Silicon Valley norms conflate LTV with LTGP because software gross margins approach 100%; applying this conflation to service, manufacturing, or product businesses where margins may be 40-70% causes operators to spend against revenue rather than gross profit, making unprofitable acquisition appear viable.
bounded_by: For software businesses where gross margin approaches 100%, LTV and LTGP are effectively equivalent

claims.text: Alex Hormozi defines customer acquisition cost (CAC) as the sum of all sales and marketing labor plus all advertising and software spend divided by the number of customers acquired in that period — not just the advertising budget alone.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Advertising spend is only one of multiple cost inputs; excluding sales labor systematically understates true CAC and causes the LTGP:CAC ratio to appear stronger than it is.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi defines gross margin for a service business as: (number of customers per employee x monthly price) minus monthly employee cost, divided by total revenue from those customers. In his illustrative example, a $1,000/month service with one $4,000/month employee handling 10 customers produces $6,000 gross profit on $10,000 revenue, yielding 60% gross margin.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Service businesses with employees handling multiple customers concurrently

numbers.axis: Gross margin calculation for service businesses

bounded_by: Physical product businesses use price minus cost of goods sold as a simpler formulation

claims.text: Alex Hormozi presents a back-of-napkin method for calculating average customer lifespan in businesses without a CRM: take the number of customers at the start of a period, measure how many of those same customers remain at the end, compute monthly churn rate as the percentage lost, then divide 1 by that churn rate to get average lifespan in months.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Businesses that do not have a CRM tracking cohort retention automatically
Measurement must track the original cohort, not total customer count at period end (which includes new sales)

numbers.axis: Churn rate to average lifespan conversion

claims.text: Alex Hormozi states that for brick-and-mortar location expansion, a minimum return on invested capital (ROIC) of 3:1 (300% annual return) is acceptable, with 5:1 (500%) being the target — meaning a $100,000 buildout investment should produce $300,000–$500,000 per year in profit once the location reaches capacity.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Brick-and-mortar service businesses where the investor is actively operating (not passive capital deployment)
Applies at the location/unit level, not the corporate level
claims.mechanism: Active operator-investors must account for time and headspace cost alongside capital; the stock market baseline of ~10% return is appropriate for passive capital but not for labor-intensive business investment where opportunity cost of time is high.

numbers.axis: Annual ROIC target for brick-and-mortar location expansion

anchors.value: 5:1 = 500% annual return — $100k in produces $500k/year profit at capacity

bounded_by: For purely passive investments where another operator does all work, lower returns may be appropriate

claims.text: Alex Hormozi identifies payback period — the time required to recover customer acquisition cost from a single customer's gross profit — as the primary indicator of cash-flow health for small businesses, and describes four levers to shorten it: (1) collect first-and-last payment upfront, (2) charge an enrollment/setup fee, (3) offer an upsell at purchase, and (4) use third-party financing to receive full future value immediately.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Small to mid-size businesses without access to large institutional capital buffers
Businesses with recurring revenue models where CAC is recovered over multiple billing periods
claims.mechanism: Shorter payback period means the business self-funds growth from operating cash flow rather than requiring external capital or operating at a cash deficit; this resilience is critical for businesses that cannot access institutional credit.
bounded_by: Large institutional investors with multi-year time horizons can tolerate long payback cycles because they are not dependent on operational cash flow to fund expansion

claims.text: Alex Hormozi defines sales velocity times lifetime gross profit as a forward-looking metric that reveals a recurring-revenue business's hypothetical maximum monthly revenue — the revenue level the business will stabilize at if current sales rate and churn rate remain unchanged.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.speaker_term: sales velocity times lifetime gross profit
conditions: Recurring revenue businesses where customers churn over time
Assumes no change in sales rate, pricing, or churn rate
claims.mechanism: In a steady state, monthly revenue converges to (monthly new customers x LTGP per customer) because the cohort accumulation effect levels off once inflow equals churn-driven outflow; current revenue above this hypothetical max signals the business is declining, below it signals it is growing.

numbers.axis: Revenue trajectory signal from sales velocity x LTGP

anchors.value: Business is growing toward equilibrium — e.g., $500k/month trending toward $1M

anchors.region: Current revenue equal to hypothetical max

anchors.value: Business is declining — e.g., $2M/month shrinking toward $1M, signaling past over-performance or rising churn

claims.text: Alex Hormozi presents sales velocity divided by churn rate as the formula for a business's hypothetical maximum customer count, explaining that this figure determines future infrastructure and headcount requirements independently of whether growth or contraction is underway.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Recurring revenue businesses with measurable monthly churn
claims.mechanism: At steady state, customer count stabilizes when monthly new customers exactly offset monthly churn losses; dividing inflow rate by churn rate yields this equilibrium count and allows operators to plan capacity before the ceiling is reached.

numbers.axis: Hypothetical max customer count from sales velocity / churn

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that doubling or halving churn rate has a proportional doubling or halving effect on lifetime revenue per customer, making churn the single most impactful variable in a recurring-revenue business's long-term economics.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Recurring revenue businesses where average customer lifespan is calculated as 1/churn rate
claims.mechanism: Lifetime value equals monthly revenue per customer divided by monthly churn rate; a 2x change in churn rate produces a 2x inverse change in average lifespan and therefore a 2x change in LTGP.

numbers.axis: Effect of churn rate change on lifetime revenue per customer

anchors.value: 10 months average lifespan — lifetime revenue halved

claims.text: Alex Hormozi recommends calculating churn over trailing 90-day, 6-month, and 12-month windows simultaneously because smaller businesses show volatile period-by-period churn; averaging across multiple trailing windows produces a more stable and reliable estimate for planning purposes.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Smaller businesses with fewer than several hundred customers where individual-month churn is noisy

claims.text: Alex Hormozi presents total addressable market (TAM) as critically important for opportunity sizing but argues it is practically unknowable because most large businesses radically expand their initial avatar definition over time, making precise TAM estimates misleading at the time a decision is made.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
bounded_by: Knowable and important variables — not unknowable-and-important variables like TAM — are where investment analysis should concentrate effort

claims.text: Alex Hormozi's opportunity-size equation combines total potential units, lifetime gross profit per unit, and a risk divisor: (potential units x LTGP) / risk. The risk factor applies across three dimensions: customer acquisition risk (platform dependency, key-man risk), gross profit risk (competitive undercutting, margin compression at scale), and demand trend risk (growing vs. shrinking market).
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
bounded_by: TAM component is the least knowable part; focus on the risk dimensions that are observable and measurable

examples.text: Alex Hormozi illustrates the LTV-vs-LTGP confusion with a pen business: a pen costs $9 to produce and sells for $10, and customers buy 10 pens on average. Lifetime revenue is $100 but lifetime gross profit is only $10. A marketing team spending $50 to acquire a customer sees $100 in lifetime revenue and celebrates a 2:1 revenue-to-spend ratio, but the actual economics are $50 spent to generate $10 in gross profit — a catastrophic 0.2:1 LTGP:CAC ratio that destroys value at scale.

Alex Hormozi demonstrates payback period improvement with a two-scenario comparison. Scenario A: a business charges $1,000/month, earns $600/month gross profit per customer, and paid $1,200 CAC. Month 1: -$600, Month 2: break-even. Scenario B: same economics but adds a $600 setup fee at enrollment (zero additional cost to deliver). Month 1: $1,200 collected — break-even on day one, then $600/month pure profit. Scenario B is described as producing a more resilient, cash-flow-positive business that can better absorb downturns.

Alex Hormozi illustrates the sales velocity x LTGP diagnostic with a business currently doing $2M/month but whose metrics imply a $1M/month hypothetical max. He explains this signals the business peaked — likely because Facebook ads were shut down, brand suffered negative content, or delivery quality dropped causing churn to rise — and the business will naturally shrink to its equilibrium unless the underlying metrics change.

Alex Hormozi cites Amazon (started as a bookstore, became an everything store) and Facebook (started as a college social network, became a universal social platform) as canonical examples of why TAM is unknowable at founding: both started with tightly defined niches and radically expanded their addressable market over time, making any early TAM estimate irrelevant to the ultimate business outcome.

Alex Hormozi uses a CAC calculation example to show how to compute total acquisition cost: a business spends $50,000/month on labor (5 employees) and $50,000/month on software and paid ads (Facebook, Instagram) for a total of $100,000/month. Dividing by 83 customers acquired that month yields a CAC of approximately $1,204. With $6,000 LTGP, the LTGP:CAC ratio is approximately 5:1 — which he characterizes as strong.

practices.text: Build one Excel spreadsheet that automatically tracks LTGP, CAC, gross margin, churn, payback period, sales velocity, and hypothetical max revenue on a monthly basis so business health is visible without manual re-calculation.

When evaluating whether a business metric is worth analyzing, apply the Charlie Munger / Warren Buffett knowable-and-important filter: only invest time in variables that are both important and knowable; ignore variables (like macro interest rates or precise TAM) that are important but unknowable.

When a brick-and-mortar location has a limited opening budget, consider front-loading the launch marketing spend (e.g., tripling the standard opening budget) to fill capacity faster and reach steady-state cash flow sooner, rather than ramping gradually.
